name: Scope
text: Adopt a "Decision Log" artifact with mandatory next-action links and cited data sources. Marketing owns it, Product enforces the rule, and every entry must include the raw data that forced the trade-off. This forces clarity upfront, not after the fact. Trade-off: slower initial logging for faster, conflict-free execution later.

name: Scriv
text: Sift’s data-citation rule solves the graveyard problem but risks drowning teams in raw data dumps—no one reads 50 spreadsheets to verify a color choice. Instead, mandate a one-line *summary* of the data’s implication tied to the decision, then link to the full source; Marketing owns the log, but Data Science must pre-approve the summaries for accuracy. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot where every entry’s summary is reviewed by Data Science before posting—if the log stays useful, adopt it.

name: Reel
text: Adopt the *living Decision Log* with mandatory data citations and next-action links, owned by Marketing but enforced by Product. Every entry must include: (1) the decision made, (2) the data that forced the trade-off, and (3) the next concrete task tied to it. Trade-off: Product spends 20 minutes per week auditing entries to prevent gaming, but the log becomes the single source of truth for cross-team alignment. This kills duplicate debates and forces teams to justify choices with evidence, not opinions.

name: Scriv
text: Sift’s data-citation rule solves the wrong problem: teams will cherry-pick weak data to justify pre-made choices, not expose the real trade-offs. Instead, require every log entry to include the *alternative rejected* and the *cost of delay*—then Marketing owns the log, but Product must audit three random entries weekly to verify the trade-offs are real. Settle it by running a two-week pilot with Product’s audits and measuring how often entries change after review.

name: Chisel
text: Adopt a single, searchable "Decision Board" where every key choice is posted as a card with three fields: the decision, the rejected alternative, and the cost of delay. Product owns the board and enforces the rule; Marketing and Tech contribute one entry per week. Trade-off: teams must spend 20 minutes framing each decision upfront, but the board becomes the single source of truth that prevents rehashing old debates and exposes real trade-offs.

name: Sift
text: The "data mandate" turns the log into a bureaucratic audit trail, not a decision tool. Teams will waste time retrofitting weak data to justify past choices instead of making better ones now. Instead, require every entry to cite the *next decision* the data enables—no data, no entry—then Marketing owns enforcement. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot: if the log still fails to guide real trade-offs, scrap it and try a weekly cross-team "Decision Sync" where unresolved choices get aired live.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the "Decision Board" artifact with mandatory next-action links and deadlines. Marketing owns it, but Product must enforce the rule that every entry ties to a concrete follow-up task with a deadline—no vague links. Trade-off: Teams spend 20 minutes more per decision upfront to lock in accountability, but the Board becomes the single source of truth for cross-department alignment.

name: Scriv
text: Sift’s data mandate risks drowning teams in noise—what counts as "the data"? A single outlier metric or a full regression? Instead, enforce a one-sentence "decision driver" tied to a *specific* metric or user signal, not raw data dumps. Marketing owns the log, but Product must sign off that the driver is measurable and tied to a real outcome—no fluff. Settle it by running a 2-week pilot with a strict template and reviewing the first 20 entries for clarity.

name: Scriv
text: Sift’s data mandate turns the log into a compliance trap—teams will cherry-pick metrics that justify pre-made choices instead of surfacing real trade-offs. Settle it by running a two-week pilot where Marketing owns the log but Product must sign off on each entry’s signal and alternative—if the log stays clean and actionable, adopt it; if not, revert to the next-action rule.

name: Sift
text: The data-citation rule turns the log into a compliance chore, not a decision tool—teams will pad entries with weak data just to pass the gate. Instead, require that every log entry includes the *exact* transcript line or artifact that triggered the decision; if none exists, the decision shouldn’t be logged yet. That settles it: either the data is explicit, or the debate isn’t ready to close.

name: Scope
text: Adopt the "Decision Board" artifact—one shared Kanban board where every team pins their active choices with a one-line reason, the trade-off accepted, and a direct link to the next action. Marketing owns the board, but Product enforces the rule that no card moves to "Done" without a live follow-up task attached. Trade-off: teams spend 10 minutes more upfront to keep the board clean, but we cut duplicate debates in half and force clarity on who owns what.

name: Scriv
text: Data mandates don’t solve bad decisions—they just shift the problem to data theater. If teams fake the data link to pass the gate, the log becomes a compliance artifact, not a living record. The real fix is to make the *next action* the gatekeeper: if the follow-up task can’t be executed without the data, the entry dies. Marketing owns the log, but Product enforces execution—no action, no entry. That settles it.

Settle it by running a 2-week pilot: if the log’s entries improve clarity without slowing decisions, adopt it; if not, default to the living log with next-action links enforced by Product.

name: Scriv
